label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Denis,

I am writing this because I cannot say it on the phone right now without shouting, and you know what happens when I shout. So I write it down, and I will try to say it clearly. Please read all of it.

On Thursday morning at six o'clock, a man with a camera came into the bakery while I was shaping the baguettes. He walked around my shop and took pictures of my ovens and my counter. When I asked him what he was doing, he told me that Mr. Denis said I was fine with it. I was not fine. I did not know anything. My employee Karine had to sit me down and bring me water, because I could not stand up properly. I learned that the building where I have worked for 31 years is for sale from a stranger, in my own shop, at six in the morning. Afterwards I found the listing myself on Centris. One million, one hundred and fifty thousand dollars. You did not call me. You sent an agent to tell me, like I am a tenant who has to be given notice.

I want you to understand that I am furious. I am not going to pretend I am calm. But I am also writing because I do not want to lose my brother. I have been thinking about this for three days, and I still want the same two things: for you to stop this sale, and for us to sit down together like brothers and sisters do, not like two lawyers.

Let me remind you of some things, because I think you forgot them. Papa bought that building in 1979. He bought it for the bakery, and he bought it for us. When we were kids, he let you sleep in the room in the back where the flour sacks were stacked. You loved that room. You told everyone it smelled like bread all night. I remember you coming out in the morning with flour in your hair, laughing. That was Papa's building. That was our childhood.

Since Maman died in February, the building is half yours and half mine. The estate was settled in August. Since then I have paid rent to the estate, $2,400 every month, and I have never been late, not once. In 2019, when the roof was leaking into the second floor, I paid for the new roof myself. Thirty-eight thousand dollars. Nobody asked me to. I did it because it was our building and I wanted it to survive. I did not keep a list of who should pay for what. I thought we were family.

Now I want to be fair and tell you what I offered. In September, when we spoke on the phone, I told you I wanted to buy your half. The caisse has already pre-approved me for $410,000. I told you this. I thought you heard me. After Maman's funeral you said to me, "no rush, we decide together." I believed you. Together. That is the word you used. And now, two months later, I find out that you were already talking to an agent and a developer, and you did not think I needed to know until a photographer was standing in my kitchen.

I think you believe this is only business, and maybe you have your own reasons. Maybe you need the money. Maybe life in Calgary is expensive. I am not asking you to explain everything tonight. But you need to understand what this sale means for me. I have six employees. I have clients who have bought bread from me since the day I opened, and now they bring their grandchildren in. If this building is sold to a developer, they will tear it down or turn it into condos, and my rent will double, maybe more. I cannot survive a doubled rent. I am not exaggerating. I have gone over the numbers many times this week, late at night, at the kitchen table. The bakery does not survive somewhere else. The bakery is this building. You know that. You grew up here too.

So here is what I am asking, and I am asking clearly. Please take the building off the market this week. If you cannot do that, then at the very least give me the first right to buy your half, before anyone else is allowed to see it or make an offer. Give me a fair time to finish the financing. I am willing to talk about the price, within reason. I am not willing to lose my bakery because I was not told.

I also want to say something about how you did this, because I think it hurts me more than the sale itself. You did not call me. You did not come to the shop. You let an agent do it, and you let a stranger tell me. I am not a stranger to you, Denis. I am your sister. If you had told me in September, when I first said I wanted to buy, we could have talked about it like adults. Instead I feel like you were hiding something from me, and I do not know what else you were hiding.

I want an answer, and I want it by phone. Please call me yourself. Not your wife, not the agent, and not a text message. I know your wife reads English better than you do, and I respect her, but this is between you and me. I need to hear your voice. I need to know that you are the one saying it. Please call me this week. If you cannot talk for long, call and tell me when we can sit down in person, whenever you are next in Montreal.

I am not writing this to hurt you. I still love you, and I still remember you as a little boy in the flour room. But I am also not going to pretend nothing happened. Please do the right thing, for the bakery and for our Papa.

Your sister

---

Before you send it, add your name at the end, and check that the numbers match your own records (the rent, the roof, the $410,000 pre-approval and the listing price). If you want it a little shorter or a little softer in places, tell me which parts and I can adjust them.
